Background (from the session that started this one):
JusPrin is an AI-piloted fork of OrcaSlicer. On 2026-10-21 Kenneth decided that JusPrin gets its own Preferences window (sections Account, Agent, Appearance, 3D view, Projects & files, Updates), with OrcaSlicer's dialog still reachable through a link. Nothing Bambu Cloud-related is shown, and there are no expert options. In the built window, OrcaSlicer's update check was dropped. The "Stable releases only" row was removed, because its only job was to configure that check. Updates now shows just the version, so JusPrin needs its own update check, which this task designs. Other decisions already made: no Thinking row in Preferences, and keep the system title bar. The prefs-window session is separately finishing the harness comparison, the language-switch crash and the wipe-tower web view, so don't touch those. Kenneth prefers reports in plain English.

Task:
Design how JusPrin checks for and announces its own new versions, replacing OrcaSlicer's update check, which JusPrin does not use. This is design and research: propose, don't implement, unless Kenneth asks.

Start from:
- The Preferences window on branch `claude/musing-wing-e808a9` (worktree `C:\src\JusPrin\.claude\worktrees\musing-wing-e808a9`). Its Updates section shows only the JusPrin version. `known_update()` in `PreferencesWindow.cpp` is the placeholder JusPrin's own check will fill. The page can already show a found update.
- OrcaSlicer's update check, for reference: the `check_stable_update_only` setting, the `NewAppAvailable` notice, and how OrcaSlicer finds releases. Check with `git blame` plus `git branch -r --contains <sha> 'upstream/*'` before calling anything OrcaSlicer's (see AGENTS.md).
- `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrintIssues/NoticeKinds.cpp`, where update notices are listed as "not shown anywhere yet" and belong on Home or in Preferences.
- The "JusPrin v2" canvas (https://claude.ai/artifact/VCEppdwfT7v32W4beUxL1v), Preferences page: the boards "Updates" and "Updates · new version available".
- `agent-docs/jusprin/product-definition.md` section 2.12: update timing is the user's decision, and the agent must not install updates on its own.

Answer, in plain English:
- Where JusPrin's releases come from: the TheSpaghettiDetective/JusPrin GitHub releases, or a JusPrin feed.
- When and how often it checks.
- What is shown, where (Updates section, Home, a notice) and in which words.
- Whether test versions are offered.
- How it behaves offline or when the check fails.
- What privacy notice it needs.
- What changes on each platform (Windows installer and MSIX, macOS, Linux).

Done means a short recommendation with 2 or 3 options and the smallest code change for the chosen one. Note any OrcaSlicer-owned file it would touch, following `agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md`.

The JusPrin Windows verification box (Windows Server 2022, user `guitest`, as of 2026-09-09): no admin rights, no GPU, reached over RDP at 100% scaling. VS 2022 Build Tools, CMake and Ninja are installed; the deps live at `C:/src/JusPrin/deps/build/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local`. Main checkout `C:/src/JusPrin` is on `jusprin-newui` with a Release build in `C:/src/JusPrin/build`.

**Why:** Several handoff items were blocked on machine facts (no debugger, no admin, DPI cannot change from inside an RDP session), so knowing them up front saves a diagnostic pass.

**How to apply:**
- GL needs Mesa, and **every freshly configured CMake build tree starts without it** — nothing in CMake or the repo supplies it. Run `pwsh src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/windows-gl/provision-mesa-windows.ps1 -BuildDir <build dir> -Source C:\src\JusPrin\build\src\Release` after configuring; it copies `libgallium_wgl.dll` and `dxil.dll` (from `C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Redist\D3D\x64\`) beside every GUI exe and `opengl32.dll` into its `mesa\` subfolder. Placement is not interchangeable, and each missing file has a silent signature — both documented in "Software GL on Windows machines without a GPU" in `agent-docs/jusprin/engineering-method.md` (on `jusprin-newui` since 2026-09-13, commit `318208608f`).
- Quick recall of the signatures: no `libgallium_wgl.dll` → `glcontext not ready, postpone init`, no `got opengl version`, black canvas all session. No `dxil.dll` → d3d12 initializes, then exit `0x80070057` on the first canvas draw with nothing logged. Both verified by removing the file and re-running. With all three present, both `d3d12` (default, `4.2 … D3D12`) and `GALLIUM_DRIVER=llvmpipe` (`4.6 … llvmpipe`) render.
- `slow_bootup` only moves the dxil crash from startup to first canvas paint; it is not a workaround.
- Lesson: a clear-only WGL smoke test passed under d3d12 because clearing compiles no shader, and was wrongly read as clearing the driver. A smoke test that skips the suspect code path proves nothing about it. (That test was removed from the repo for this reason.)
- A first-run datadir (e.g. copies of `C:\b\dd3`) logs ~630k lines in the first minute — the `GuideFrame::GetFilamentInfo` profile scan, driver-independent. Not a GL symptom.
- `D3D12 (Microsoft Basic Render Driver)` in the log is **Mesa's own d3d12 gallium driver on WARP**, not Microsoft's GLon12 mapping layer and not a real GPU. Confirm which GL is live by listing the process's loaded modules: the bundled Mesa shows `<exe dir>\mesa\opengl32.dll` + `libgallium_wgl.dll` (+ `DXIL.dll` once d3d12 has drawn), the unprovisioned fallback shows only `C:\Windows\SYSTEM32\OPENGL32.dll`.
- The permission guard refuses `Remove-Item` under `C:\b` (it reports it as a protected path) and misparses `rd /s /q` and path-like string literals as delete targets. Hand build-tree deletion to the user; build trees there contain `resources` symlinks into live worktrees, so unlink those before any recursive delete.
- A debugger can be had without admin: download `https://aka.ms/windbg/download` (an .appinstaller pointing at a ~1.2 GB msixbundle), unzip the bundle, unzip `windbg_win-x64.msix`, and `amd64/cdb.exe` runs directly. Set `_NO_DEBUG_HEAP=1` when running the harness under cdb, or teardown crawls in the debug heap for many minutes.
- Fixture directories for the harness's visual modes must be short paths (e.g. `C:\Users\guitest\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\wp\...`); a long scratchpad path makes the profile-bundle copy exceed MAX_PATH and the fixture slice never validates.
- The harness prints everything on stderr; the exit code must be read with `$LASTEXITCODE` in PowerShell (bash shows 127).
- DPI at 150%/200% needs the user to reconnect the RDP session at that scale. See [[jusprin-windows-parity-handoff]].

Node is installed twice: the older `C:\tools\node` (v24.20.0), which is **not on PATH**, and
`C:\Users\guitest\.local\node-v24.21.0-win-x64` (v24.21.0, npm 11.19.0), added to the **user
PATH** on 2026-09-16. Check `Get-Command npm.cmd` before installing anything; a fresh Bash
session may still need `export PATH="$PATH:/c/Users/guitest/.local/node-v24.21.0-win-x64"`.

npm is not optional any more: since commit `5fc0efe2e3` the Agent and Home pages are built from
TypeScript and their `resources/jusprin/{agent,home}/index.html` is generated, not committed.
Without npm, CMake **fails at configure time** (`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Web/CMakeLists.txt`
`FATAL_ERROR`), so the first new source file you add breaks the build tree; and without the
bundles the app creates no Agent WebView at all, which shows up as `shell_agent_webview_created
FAIL` / "the Agent page did not complete its handshake" in the shell harness. Build them with
`npm ci && npm run build` in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI` and `HomeUI`.

# Fork stewardship

**Status:** Required discipline for every change to an upstream-owned file on `jusprin-newui`.

JusPrin is a long-lived fork. Every line it changes in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line it re-resolves at every rebase, forever, by a person who was not there when the line was written. The rules below exist to keep that permanent cost small and, where it cannot be small, to keep it visible.

One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**

- Owning *product policy* is safe. It is ours, upstream will never write it, and it lives in our files.
- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.

Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.

## The ten principles

### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much

**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.

**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.

**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?

**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.

### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge

**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.

**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.

**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?

**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.

### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it

**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.

**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.

**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?

**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. Re-expressing the vendor-specific snapshot walk silently dropped one of its branches. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.

### 4. Own the policy; borrow the mechanism

**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.

**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.

**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?

**Violation.** A product-named enum value inside a rendering class, or product decisions embedded in an upstream mouse handler. The fix is a neutral options struct plus a fork-owned controller that applies our policy.

### 5. One seam beats many touch points

**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.

**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.

**The test.** Do all the paths I am hooking already converge somewhere downstream? Is there one function that runs exactly when the thing I care about has happened?

**Violation.** Publishing a history-changed event from undo, from redo, and from both history-navigation entry points, when all four funnel through a single update function that runs only on a successful move.

### 6. One shared implementation is worth a guaranteed conflict

**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.

**Mechanism.** A conflict is a stop; drift between two copies is silent and unbounded. Trading an invisible risk for a visible, small, recurring one is a good trade.

**The test.** Where did the logic I removed actually go? A move has one implementation; only a duplication risks divergence. If I wrote new behavior beside an existing upstream path rather than calling it, upstream's future improvements will never reach our users.

**Violation.** Writing a second object-duplication routine next to OrcaSlicer's clipboard path and pointing an existing dialog at it. Reusing the existing path — extending it where it was too narrow — keeps one implementation.

### 7. Unavoidable conflicts must be easy to resolve correctly

**Rule.** When you must delete or relocate an upstream line, say at the site what moved, where it went, and what a future rebase must carry across.

**Mechanism.** The real cost of a conflict is not the stop; it is the chance of resolving it wrongly. Appending near an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — keep both — is right. Deleting an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — take mine, the logic moved — silently discards whatever upstream did to that line in the meantime.

**The test.** Six months from now, is the natural resolution of the conflict I am creating the correct one? If not, what does the resolver need to read to get it right, and is that text next to the conflict?

**Violation.** Removing an upstream snapshot label that upstream later localized. Git stops for a human, but the intent-faithful resolution throws the translation away, and nothing at the site says otherwise.

### 8. Do not diverge where you gain nothing; converge where upstream already went

**Rule.** No gratuitous formatting, reordering, or whitespace differences. Before reverting a cosmetic difference, compare against current upstream — it may have made the same change.

**Mechanism.** Every valueless difference is a conflict site that buys nothing. And if upstream has independently arrived at your version, "fixing" it back creates divergence rather than removing it. Adopting a change upstream has already made converges the two trees early and makes the eventual conflict resolve itself.

**The test.** Does this difference carry meaning? Has upstream already made it?

**Violation.** Consuming a shared blank line in a list of build subdirectories, where upstream also appends entries.

### 9. Verify the risk claim instead of reasoning about it

**Rule.** Before asserting that a change is or is not rebase-risky, check it. Three checks, each one command: does git actually conflict there; has upstream already converged on the same change; is the change a move or a duplication.

**Mechanism.** A coherent story about fork risk is not a true one, and every one of these is cheaper to check than to argue about. Reasoning alone reliably produces confident, wrong claims — that a lost change is "silent" when git stops for it, that a move is a "duplication," that a cosmetic difference is gratuitous when upstream shares it.

**The test.** Did I run the simulation, or am I describing what I expect it to say?

**Violation.** A report that lists which files are rebase-sensitive and calls the change narrow, without having run the merge simulation that would have found two lossy resolutions waiting in it.

### 10. Pull direction dominates every local edit

**Rule.** Replay the fork's own commits onto upstream. Never merge upstream in, and never rebase the whole branch.

**Mechanism.** The fork's own footprint is small; the inherited release-branch history is not. Merging upstream in makes the conflict surface the entire divergence between the release branch and upstream's development line — none of it ours. Rebasing only our commits discards that inherited history by taking upstream's version of every file we never touched.

**The test.** Am I replaying our commits onto upstream, or bringing upstream into ours?

**Violation.** `git merge upstream/main`, which produces a conflict list dominated by vendor profiles, translations, and CI files that JusPrin has never edited.

## Before you finish

A change that touches upstream-owned files is not done until this is recorded in the handback or pull request:

1. **The rebase simulation and its result.** Run it against current upstream and name both endpoint commits — measurements are not reproducible otherwise.

   ```bash
   git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<fork base> upstream/main HEAD
   ```

   For each conflicted file, state whether the natural resolution is correct or lossy. A lossy one is a defect to fix now, not a note for later.

2. **An account of every upstream line deleted or rewritten.** Where the logic went, and why an additive form was not possible.

3. **A statement of what the fork now owns.** Policy, a neutral seam, or upstream behavior. The third needs an explicit justification.

An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It is not proof that a future rebase will merge, and never proof that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the focused contract tests, the full native build, the real multi-plate workflow, native gizmo input, and the stock-behavior regression checks.

## This fork's terrain

Facts specific to OrcaSlicer, worth knowing before choosing where to put a seam. They change over time; re-measure rather than trusting these.

`Plater.cpp` is by far the busiest file the fork touches, followed by the central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt`, `GLCanvas3D.cpp`, and `PartPlate.cpp`. `GLToolbar` and `GLGizmosManager` are quiet. File-level churn is only a first approximation: some functions inside `Plater.cpp` have not been touched upstream in the entire life of this fork, and a seam there is far cheaper than the file's overall rate suggests. Measure the function, not just the file.

Some native state is shared rather than owned by one object. OrcaSlicer's collapse toolbar belongs to `Plater` and is used by both the Prepare and Preview canvases, so a per-canvas guard cannot save and restore it correctly. Shared state needs one owner at the shared lifetime boundary, and exact restoration needs a getter as well as a setter.

`MainFrame`'s Notebook is cheaper to wrap than to dismantle. Dozens of
upstream predicates — menu and shortcut enabling, `can_delete`, slice status
updates, undo/redo gating — key off `m_tabpanel->GetSelection()`, so removing
or reparenting the Prepare/Preview pages breaks them with no conflict and no
error. A shell gets a tabless full-window layout for free instead: hide the
strip via the public `GetBtnsListCtrl()` (wxBookCtrlBase gives a hidden
controller zero size, so pages fill the client area), and the stock slice and
print side buttons disappear with it because `ButtonsListCtrl` reparents them

# JusPrin's own update check: design (2026-10-22)

Design only. Nothing implemented. Worktree read: musing-wing-e808a9 @ 95ab4ea1c2.

## What is true today (checked)

- **JusPrin shows OrcaSlicer's update pop-up.** I ran the prf build (`C:\b\prf\src\Release\orca-slicer.exe`) with a copy of `C:\b\dd3`. Ten seconds in, the "New version of Orca Slicer" window opened and offered "OrcaSlicer V2.5.0 Alpha", with a "Check on GitHub" link to OrcaSlicer. Screenshot: `update-check-orca-dialog-in-jusprin.png` in this folder.
  Why it happens: `GUI_App` startup calls `check_new_version_sf()`. That asks `check-version.orcaslicer.com/latest`. `check_stable_update_only` defaults to false, so the alpha counts, and 2.5.0-alpha is newer than 2.4.2.
- That request also sends OrcaSlicer an install ID (`iid`), plus the version, OS, architecture and OS description. It goes out even in stealth mode. All of this is upstream code: the same text is in upstream/main. Blame can't show it, because the fork's history starts at a squashed root commit, 56eb9a1a46, with no merge-base.
- JusPrin has no version number of its own. `SoftFever_VERSION` is "2.4.2", which is OrcaSlicer's, so Preferences says "JusPrin 2.4.2". JusPrin v1 (origin/main) set it to 1.4.0 and still asked OrcaSlicer's server, according to its code. I did not run v1.
- JusPrin's GitHub releases: `jusprin/v1.4.0` (2025-10-19, the latest stable), v1.3.0, and older `v*` tags. There is also a rolling `nightly-builds` pre-release with Windows exe and zip, macOS dmg, AppImage and flatpak files. No v2 release yet. The CI publish steps are gated to the OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer repo.
- MSIX: `scripts/msix` and its CI step are OrcaSlicer's, and the identity is OrcaSlicer's. JusPrin ships no MSIX.
- Canvas boards: "Updates" shows "JusPrin [VERSION]", "Up to date · checked [TIME]" and [Check now]. "Updates · new version available" shows "JusPrin [NEW] is available", "You have [VERSION]. Your projects and settings carry over.", [Download] and [What's new], plus a dot on the Updates nav item. The built page has the "available" card and the dot, but no checked line and no Check now.

## Recommendation: option 1

JusPrin's own small check, reading GitHub releases. OrcaSlicer's check is handed over through one neutral hook.

- Source: `GET https://api.github.com/repos/TheSpaghettiDetective/JusPrin/releases?per_page=30`. Skip drafts and pre-releases. Tags are `v<semver>` or `jusprin/v<semver>`. Pick the highest version above the running one. Its `html_url` is the Download and What's new link.
- When: at startup, if the last check is more than 24 h old (OrcaSlicer's startup call reaches it through the hook). Once a day while JusPrin stays open. Any time from Check now. Timeouts 5 s connect, 10 s total.
- Shown:
  - In Preferences, as on the canvas.
  - On Home, one quiet strip: "JusPrin X is available." with Download, What's new and ×. × hides it until a newer version.
  - Nothing modal, nothing in projects or chat. The agent never downloads or installs.
- Test versions: no. A build that is itself a test version (2.1.0-beta1) is told about newer test versions. Nightly builds are never offered.
- Offline or a failed check: silent. Preferences says "Couldn't check just now · last checked …". The next try is at the next start or 24 h later. A failure is recorded as a failure, never as "up to date". Don't copy OrcaSlicer's `catch (...) {}`.
- Privacy: a plain GET with no install ID and no OS details. GitHub sees the IP address and the User-Agent "JusPrin/<version>". Add a check row in "What to check for", on by default: "New JusPrin versions — Once a day JusPrin asks GitHub for its list of releases. GitHub sees your IP address, as with any web page. Nothing about you or your projects is sent." It is also off when stealth mode is on.
- Platforms:
  - Windows exe and zip, macOS dmg and AppImage: same check; Download opens the release page.
  - MSIX, if it ever ships: no check, and the page says "Updates come from the Microsoft Store" (use upstream's `is_running_in_msix()`).
  - Flatpak from a store, later: same idea, using `/.flatpak-info` as upstream does.

## Smallest code change

1. The OrcaSlicer-owned files are touched in one place, three lines, all additive:
   - `GUI_App.hpp`: `std::function<void(int by_user)> app_update_check; // runs instead of the built-in check when set`
   - First line of `GUI_App::check_new_version_sf()`: `if (app_update_check) { app_update_check(by_user); return; }`
   - The function has had one upstream commit since 2026-01. JusPrin sets the hook in `JusPrin::attach_shell()`, which runs in the MainFrame constructor, before the startup CallAfter.
   - Classic view's "Check for updates" menu item then runs JusPrin's check instead of doing nothing.
   - The rebase simulation must be run when this is implemented.
2. New files `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Updates/UpdateCheck.{hpp,cpp}`. They hold a pure `choose_update(releases json, running version)`, tested in tests/jusprin, and the request plus app_config state: version, url, checked time, last result, dismissed version. They borrow upstream's `Http` and `Semver`.
3. `JUSPRIN_VERSION` goes in a fork-owned cmake file. Leave `SoftFever_VERSION` alone: profiles, the `user_backup-v<ver>` folder and the conf "version" depend on it. Kenneth picks the first v2 number, which must be above 1.4.0.
4. In `PreferencesWindow.cpp`, `known_update()` reads UpdateCheck, and a `check_now` effect is added. Preferences.tsx and protocol.ts get the checked line, Check now, the failure line and the toggle.
5. The Home strip needs a canvas board first.

## Options not chosen

- **Option 2: reuse OrcaSlicer's check.** Point its `version_check_url` setting at JusPrin's GitHub API and bind `EVT_SLIC3R_VERSION_ONLINE` later so JusPrin's handler swallows the event. It adds the fewest lines. But it sends the install ID and OS details to GitHub on every check, and it keeps OrcaSlicer's test-version logic and its by-user dialogs. It also depends on the order wx calls event handlers in, which upstream can change with no merge conflict.
- **Option 3: a JusPrin feed on Obico's server.** It gives the most control: pulling a bad release, staged rollout, per-platform links, a message. But it needs a server and a step to keep it in sync with GitHub releases, and the privacy line must name Obico. Option 1 keeps the URL in one constant, so moving later is cheap.

I've written the design for JusPrin's own update check; nothing is implemented. While researching it I found a live problem: **JusPrin opens OrcaSlicer's update window at startup.** The full design is in `update-check-design.md` in the shared notes folder, next to a screenshot of that window.

**What happens today**
- I ran the Preferences build with a copy of a normal data folder. About 10 seconds after start, a window titled "New version of Orca Slicer" opened, offering "OrcaSlicer V2.5.0 Alpha" with a "Check on GitHub" link. The startup check asks OrcaSlicer's server, test versions are on by default, and 2.5.0-alpha counts as newer than 2.4.2.
- That check also sends OrcaSlicer a lasting install ID, the version, the operating system and the processor type, even in stealth mode. This is all upstream code: the same text is in OrcaSlicer's main branch. `git blame` can't show it, because the fork's history starts at one squashed commit.
- JusPrin has no version number of its own. "2.4.2" is OrcaSlicer's number, so Preferences says "JusPrin 2.4.2". Going by its code, JusPrin v1 asked OrcaSlicer's server too; I didn't run v1.

**Recommendation: option 1, a small check of JusPrin's own that reads JusPrin's GitHub releases**
- **Where releases come from:** the release list of TheSpaghettiDetective/JusPrin on GitHub. It skips drafts and test releases, reads tags like `v2.1.0` and `jusprin/v1.4.0`, and takes the highest version above the one running. The release page is what Download and "What's new" open.
- **When it checks:** at startup if the last check was more than a day ago, once a day while JusPrin stays open, and whenever the person clicks "Check now".
- **What is shown:**
  - Preferences › Updates looks like the canvas: "JusPrin 2.0.0 · Up to date · checked 2 hours ago" with Check now, or "JusPrin 2.1.0 is available. You have 2.0.0. Your projects and settings carry over." with Download and What's new, and a dot on the Updates item.
  - Home gets one quiet strip: "JusPrin 2.1.0 is available." with Download, What's new and ×. Closing it hides it until an even newer version comes out.
  - No pop-up, nothing inside a project or the chat, and the agent never downloads or installs anything.
- **Test versions:** not offered. The one exception is someone already running a test build, who hears about newer test builds. The rolling nightly builds have no version number, so they are never offered.
- **Offline or a failed check:** nothing pops up. Preferences says "Couldn't check just now · last checked 3 days ago", and the next try is at the next start or a day later. A failure is never reported as "up to date".
- **Privacy notice:** the request sends nothing about the person. GitHub sees the IP address and "JusPrin/<version>", as for any web request JusPrin makes. I'd add a row to "What to check for", on by default:
  - Title: "New JusPrin versions"
  - Text: "Once a day JusPrin asks GitHub for its list of releases. GitHub sees your IP address, as with any web page. Nothing about you or your projects is sent."

  The row also counts as off when stealth mode is on.
- **Platforms:**
  - The Windows installer and zip, the macOS .dmg and the Linux AppImage all work the same way: Download opens the release page and the person installs the new version themselves.
  - JusPrin ships no Microsoft Store (MSIX) package today; that setup is still OrcaSlicer's. If one ships, it skips the check and says "Updates come from the Microsoft Store".
  - A Flatpak installed from a software store would be handled the same way.

**The other two options**
- **Option 2, point OrcaSlicer's check at JusPrin's releases:** it needs the fewest new lines. But it keeps sending the install ID and system details, keeps OrcaSlicer's test-version logic and windows, and depends on an event-handling order that a future OrcaSlicer change could break with no merge conflict.
- **Option 3, a JusPrin feed on Obico's server:** most control, such as pulling a bad release, a gradual rollout or per-platform links. But it needs a server and a step to keep it in sync with GitHub, and the privacy notice would have to name Obico. Option 1 keeps the address in one place, so moving to this later is cheap.

**Smallest code change for option 1**
1. **One OrcaSlicer-owned spot**, three added lines and none removed:
   - `GUI_App.hpp` gets a neutral hook: when it is set, it runs instead of OrcaSlicer's built-in update check.
   - The first line of `check_new_version_sf()` calls the hook and returns.
   - JusPrin sets the hook in `attach_shell()`, which runs before the startup check.

   That reuses OrcaSlicer's startup timing, and makes classic view's "Check for updates" run JusPrin's check. Upstream has changed that function once this year. The rebase check that `fork-stewardship.md` asks for still has to be run when this is built.
2. **New JusPrin files** `JusPrin/Updates/UpdateCheck.{hpp,cpp}`. They hold a small "pick the newest release" function with tests, plus the request and the saved result. They reuse OrcaSlicer's existing web-request and version-comparison code.
3. **A JusPrin version number** in a fork-owned build file. OrcaSlicer's number stays as it is, because profiles and backup folders depend on it.
4. **The Preferences window:** `known_update()` reads the result, and the page gains "Check now", the "checked …" line, the failure line and the new row.
5. **A canvas board for the Home strip.** The canvas has none yet, so it needs designing first.

**Decisions for you**
- Is option 1 the one to build?
- Should the OrcaSlicer pop-up be switched off now, ahead of the rest? The hook alone does that.
- JusPrin v2's first version number. It must be above 1.4.0 and separate from OrcaSlicer's 2.4.2.

we can use our own release list of TheSpaghettiDetective/JusPrin on GitHub.. but The upstream updates dialogue is ugly, there's no reason to reuse it. design our own update dialog experience on the preferences page

I've designed JusPrin's own update experience in the Preferences window's Updates section, on the **JusPrin v2 canvas**: https://claude.ai/artifact/VCEppdwfT7v32W4beUxL1v (page "Agent setup & Preferences"). The new row is called "Updates · from Check now to Restart and install". Nothing is built in the app, and I haven't looked at the boards rendered on the canvas.

**One area, one card that changes with each state.** No pop-ups, and OrcaSlicer's update window isn't used at all.
- **Up to date:** "JusPrin 2.0.0 · Up to date · checked 2 hours ago", with a **Check now** button.
- **Checking:** "Looking for a newer version on GitHub…", with a small moving bar. The button turns into a greyed-out "Checking…".
- **Couldn't check:** "Couldn't reach GitHub · last checked 3 days ago", with **Try again**. A grey line says JusPrin tries again tomorrow or the next time it starts. The dot is amber, not red, because being offline isn't an error.
- **New version available:** "JusPrin 2.1.0 is available · Released [date] · you have 2.0.0".
  - The release notes from the GitHub release appear right in the card, in a short scrolling box, with a link to the full notes on GitHub.
  - The main button is **Download and install**, with the file size beside it. **Skip this version** hides that version until a newer one comes out.
- **Downloading:** a progress bar, "[done] of [size] MB · keep working, or close this window", and **Cancel**.
- **Ready to install:** "JusPrin 2.1.0 is ready to install. JusPrin saves your projects, closes, installs the new version and opens again." The button is **Restart and install**, with "Not now? It waits here until you are ready."
- **Download didn't finish:** "The connection dropped at 38 of 112 MB. Nothing was installed." The options are **Try again** or "Download from GitHub instead".
- **Microsoft Store install:** "Updates come from the Microsoft Store", with no check.

**Other changes in the section**
- The "Stable releases only" row is gone, matching the built window.
- A new checkbox, "New JusPrin versions", is on by default. Its text doubles as the privacy notice: "Once a day JusPrin asks GitHub for its list of releases. GitHub sees your IP address, as with any web page. Nothing about you or your projects is sent."
- The dot on the Updates item in the side list shows while a version is waiting, downloading or ready to install.
- The main Preferences board is clickable in Play: Check now leads to checking, then the new version, then Download and install, then downloading, then ready. There's also a dark-mode board of the "new version" state.

**Decisions for you**
1. **Installing inside the app is new work.**
   - Behind the scenes, JusPrin picks the right file for the computer and checks it against the checksum GitHub publishes for each release file.
   - On Windows, "Restart and install" runs the installer after JusPrin quits.
   - On macOS it can only open the disk image, so the person still drags JusPrin into Applications.
   - Portable and Flatpak copies fall back to "Download from GitHub".
   
   If that's too much for the first version, the same card can make **Download** open the GitHub release page and drop the downloading and ready states.
2. **JusPrin's first v2 version number.** The check compares version numbers, and today JusPrin reports OrcaSlicer's 2.4.2. The new number has to be above v1's 1.4.0.
3. **Switching off OrcaSlicer's update window**, which still opens at startup offering OrcaSlicer 2.5.0 Alpha. Turning it off needs the three-line change in OrcaSlicer's `GUI_App` from my first report; it can go in now, before the rest is built.

content.text:
JusPrin no longer opens OrcaSlicer's "New version of Orca Slicer" window at startup. The fix is commit `a6cf684da9` on branch `claude/no-orca-update-window`, cut from `jusprin-newui` (worktree `.claude/worktrees/no-orca-update-window`), and only JusPrin's own files changed.

**What I changed**
- A small JusPrin event filter (`JusPrin/Shell/OrcaUpdateFilter.{hpp,cpp}`) throws away the "new version found" event from OrcaSlicer's check before anything can open the window. It logs "Not offering OrcaSlicer <version>" when it does.
- A filter runs before every other handler, so the fix doesn't depend on which side registered first.
- `attach_shell()`, the existing JusPrin startup point, installs it before its other checks, so classic view is covered too. Each main window owns its filter and removes it when it closes, so recreating the window (on a language change) doesn't leave extras behind.
- I added `test_orca_update_filter.cpp` to `shell_theme_tests`; it checks the event is dropped and other events pass through.

**Why not the routes suggested**
- **The settings OrcaSlicer's check reads:** I didn't find one that works. "Stable releases only" would hide the window only until OrcaSlicer ships a stable release above 2.4.2. Pointing the check at another address would still show OrcaSlicer's window, for whatever releases that address lists.
- **OrcaSlicer's `GUI_App`:** not needed, so nothing for the rebase check in `fork-stewardship.md`.

**How I confirmed it, each with its own copy of `C:\b\dd3`**
- The unfixed build (`C:\b\prf`) opened "New version of Orca Slicer" 15 seconds after start.
- The fixed build showed only the main window for 40 seconds, and its log says `Not offering OrcaSlicer 2.5.0.0-alpha`, so the check did run and the filter stopped it.
- On the fixed build's first run there was neither a window nor that log line, so I can't tell from it whether the check had completed. The second run is the one that shows the filter at work.
- All of `shell_theme_tests` passes: 351 checks, including the new two.

**What this doesn't fix**
- **OrcaSlicer's request still goes out.** It sends OrcaSlicer's server an install ID, the version and system details at every start, and JusPrin's own check won't change that. Stopping it needs the small additive change to `GUI_App` from my first report.
- **Help › Check for Updates in OrcaSlicer's menu.** When OrcaSlicer has a newer release, clicking it now does nothing visible. When it doesn't, it still says "This is the newest version."

**Build notes**
- While the disk was full, the link failed. I deleted the two precompiled-header files in my own build tree and linked the app without a debug-symbols file. Every later build ran with plenty of space.
- `C:\b\nouw` is about 13 GB and can be deleted once this is merged.
